title: How Many Roberts Do You Know
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers a quick, name-based trick for estimating the size of one's personal network, attributed to researcher Tyler McCormick at the University of Washington. Because roughly 1% of Americans share a name like Robert, counting how many Roberts you know well and multiplying by 100 gives a rough estimate of overall network size. The author frames this as more than a parlor trick, tying it to career outcomes and citing LinkedIn research showing that acquaintances matter more than close friends for finding new jobs. For sales and fundraising teams especially, the piece argues, network size is a real predictor of success worth estimating deliberately.
points: A simple name-based trick estimates personal network size using common names like Robert.
Counting known Roberts (or similar common names) and multiplying by roughly 100 approximates network size.
LinkedIn research shows acquaintances matter more than close friends for finding new jobs.
For sales and fundraising teams, network size is a meaningful predictor of success.
quotes: Who you know really matters, and as your network grows, so does the probability of good fortune.
There are roughly 4.3 million Americans named Robert, which is just over 1% of the population.
If you know 10 Roberts well enough to have their contact information and to have had a conversation with them in the past two years, then you likely have a personal network of 1,000 people.
Nothing produces opportunities like an ever-expanding network.
As personal networks expand during a career, so do learning opportunities, job offers, invitations to attend life-shaping events, and occasions to be a part of special experiences.
So, estimating the size of your personal network and those of your team members can be an illuminating exercise.

For those teams and team members dependent on an expanding network to achieve goals, such as sales and fund-raising teams, assessing how many people an individual knows and connects with is often a predictor of success.
Unfortunately, accurate estimates of personal networks are difficult to come by.
